content: Bayraktar Lab / Wellcome Sanger Institute News Collaboration Science Cellular Genomics Uncovering rules for aggressive brain tumours could lead to better treatments News article by the Communications Team 4 Nov 2026 Aggressive brain tumours follow predictable rules, not chaotic randomness, according to new research. This discovery could lead to new, much needed ways to treat glioblastoma tumours in the future. Email newsletter News and blog updates Sign up Researchers at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the European Molecular Biology Laboratory (EMBL), the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute, the Francis Crick Institute, and their collaborators, have mapped over one million cells across glioblastoma tumours. This allowed them to discover that the cancer cells organise themselves according to a consistent, predictable structural pattern across different patients. In this new study, published today (4 November) in Nature , the team was able to categorise cancer cells at different stages of their journey within the different environments in glioblastoma tumours. They looked at different time stages and used lab-grown mini tumours to mimic this development. Along with challenging previously held beliefs about brain tumours, this roadmap opens new paths for developing targeted treatments. As the cancer cells move along in a predictable way during tumour progression, future drugs could specifically target the early developmental-like cells before they transform into harder-to-reach, resistant states. This work has built a new foundational resource for studies to explore the mechanisms and biology of cancerous brain cells. For example, using the same single-cell multi-omic data, generated jointly for both studies, researchers also decoded the gene regulators that drive and restrict glioblastoma cell state transitions, highlighting potential targets that could help avoid treatment resistance. These results are published today in a companion paper in Nature 1 . Together, these papers unify understanding of the architecture of glioblastomas with insights about cancer cell plasticity, giving a holistic view of this cancer type. Glioblastoma is an aggressive form of brain cancer. It is the most common type of brain cancer in adults, with around 3,200 people being diagnosed every year in the UK. The average survival time for people with glioblastoma is 12 to 18 months, with only 4 per cent of those diagnosed surviving five years or more 2 . When possible, the most common glioblastoma treatment is surgery, followed by a combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy 3 . These tumours are difficult to treat due to their location and as many tumours invade multiple parts of the brain, which can make surgery difficult or impossible in some cases. Heidi Halls, from West Sussex, lost her dad, Steve Grant, to glioblastoma in February last year (2025). “When Dad was diagnosed, we were told treatment wasn’t an option and that he had just 12 weeks to live. We were left with so many questions: why had this happened to him? What was happening inside his brain? What would change next, and what would those changes mean? Watching him lose his memory, hallucinate and struggle with everyday things was utterly devastating. We needed help to understand what he was experiencing and how best to support him. Even now, I am still trying to make sense of what happened. Research is urgently needed to understand this disease and develop better treatments. But families also need clear explanations, compassionate guidance and support throughout. When treatment isn’t possible, that need is still there. Being told there is nothing that can be done to treat the tumour must never mean there is nothing more that can be done for the person and their family.” Heidi Halls speaking about her dad Steve, pictured left How can research help? Glioblastoma treatment can also be difficult as these tumours are made up of multiple, highly dynamic cancer cell states that previously did not seem to follow any consistent rules or patterns. This means that treatment might not destroy every cell, leading to drug resistance and cancer re-emergence. In a new study, Sanger Institute researchers and their collaborators used state of the art multi-omic technologies and tailored machine learning computational tools to map multiple sections of brain tumour samples from 12 glioblastoma patients 4 , combining single-cell and spatial atlassing, imaging, and whole-genome sequencing data. This range of information gives a complete understanding of each cancer cell’s molecular state, where it is in the tumour, how it is likely to change over time, how it interacts with the environment around it, and its genetic information. Additionally, the team used samples from multiple regions of the brain tumours, to give a full picture of the cells in each tumour section and how they related to each other.
